title: MOSES GAVE GOD EXCUSE AFTER EXCUSE—UNTIL THE BIBLE SAYS GOD BECAME ANGRY
paragraphs: MOSES GAVE GOD EXCUSE AFTER EXCUSE—UNTIL THE BIBLE SAYS GOD BECAME ANGRY

He survived Pharaoh’s death sentence, murdered a man, fled into the wilderness, and spent forty years hiding from the life he once knew. But when God finally called his name from a burning bush, Moses kept saying no. And the most frightening part of this story may not be God's anger. It may be how much of Moses we recognize in ourselves.
There is a moment in Exodus that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Not because Moses committed murder.
Not because he ran away.
Not even because he questioned whether he was qualified to lead an entire nation out of slavery.
But because after God answered his fears, revealed His name, promised His presence, and gave him miraculous signs, Moses still wanted someone else to go.
And then Scripture says something we rarely hear preached with the weight it deserves.
“And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses.” — Exodus 4:14, KJV
Read that again.
God was not angry because Moses was weak.
God was not angry because Moses had questions.
God had patiently answered his questions, addressed his inadequacy, and promised to be with him.
But Moses eventually reached the point where his objections exposed something deeper than insecurity.
He did not want to go.
And before you judge him, consider the prayers you have prayed while quietly hoping God would never ask you to act on them.
“Lord, use me.”
But not if it costs my comfort.
“Lord, change me.”
But not if I have to surrender what I secretly love.
“Lord, send me.”
But not if the people who remember my past are waiting on the other side.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing standing between us and obedience is not the devil, our enemies, or our circumstances.
Sometimes it is the excuse we have rehearsed so many times that it finally sounds like wisdom.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because Moses was not standing before a God who did not understand his history.
He was standing before the only One who knew every chapter of it.
Every failure.
Every regret.
Every buried memory.
Every fear he had carried into the wilderness.
And God called him anyway.
Before there was a burning bush, there was a basket floating on the Nile.
Moses entered the world under a death sentence.
Pharaoh had commanded that Hebrew baby boys be thrown into the river. His mother hid him as long as she could, then placed him in a basket among the reeds.
Imagine being a mother whose act of love required letting go of her child.
Imagine the trembling hands.
The river moving.
The silence after she released that basket.
She could not see the entire future.
But God was not absent from that river.
Pharaoh's own daughter discovered the child, took pity on him, and raised him within the household connected to the very regime that had ordered his death.
The boy who should have died grew up in the shadow of Egyptian power.
Yet his identity was never simply Egyptian.
He belonged to the people who were suffering.
And one day, the tension between those two worlds erupted.
Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew man.
He looked around.
Then he killed the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.
Exodus 2:12 records the act without disguising its violence.
The next day, Moses tried to intervene between two fighting Hebrews, only to hear a question that must have pierced him.
“Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?” — Exodus 2:14, KJV
Then came the accusation.
Would he kill them too?
His secret was no longer secret.
Pharaoh sought his life.
Moses fled.
The man who had grown up around royalty became a fugitive in Midian.
He married, became a father, and worked as a shepherd.
The book of Acts later describes Moses as forty years old when he visited his people and eighty when he stood before Pharaoh (Acts 7:23; 7:30; Exodus 7:7).
Forty years in Egypt.
Approximately forty years away.
Four decades between the disaster he left behind and the calling that awaited him.
Think about what forty years can do to a person.
Forty years can make disappointment feel permanent.
Forty years can turn an abandoned dream into something you no longer dare to mention.
Forty years can teach you to live small enough that nobody expects anything from you.
Perhaps Moses had made peace with the thought that his greatest opportunity was already buried in Egypt.
Perhaps he believed the wilderness was where he would die.
Scripture does not tell us everything he thought during those years.
But it tells us what happened when God interrupted them.
One ordinary day, Moses led his flock toward Horeb, the mountain of God.
There he saw a bush burning with fire.
Yet the bush was not consumed.
He turned aside to investigate.
And from the midst of the fire, God called:
“Moses, Moses.” — Exodus 3:4, KJV
Notice something beautiful.
God did not begin by calling him murderer.
Fugitive.
Failure.
Coward.
Disappointment.
He called him by name.
That does not mean Moses' sin was insignificant. It means his failure had not placed him beyond God's sovereign purpose.
Moses answered, “Here am I.”
In Hebrew, the expression is הִנֵּנִי — hinnēnî, meaning “Here I am.”
It is the language of personal presence and availability.
But being present before God and being ready to obey everything He says are not always the same thing.
Moses would soon discover that.
God commanded him to remove his sandals because the place where he stood was holy ground.
Then God identified Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses hid his face.
He was afraid to look upon God.
And then the Lord spoke about something that had been happening far away in Egypt.
The suffering of His people.
Their oppression.
Their cries.
Their bondage.
God declared:
“I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows.” — Exodus 3:7, KJV
The Hebrew wording carries remarkable force.
רָאֹה רָאִיתִי — rāʾōh rāʾîtî
Literally, the construction emphasizes seeing: “I have surely seen.”
God was not casually observing their suffering.
He was declaring that their affliction had not escaped His attention.
Then He said He had heard their cry.
And He knew their sorrows.
Seen.
Heard.
Known.
Three truths that must have sounded like rain on the dry ground of generations of slavery.
Perhaps you need those words today.
Because there are forms of suffering people never notice.
You can sit in church and smile while your marriage is quietly falling apart.
You can post Scriptures while fighting a temptation you are ashamed to confess.
You can encourage everyone around you and still cry when nobody is watching.
You can spend years serving God while wondering whether He has forgotten the prayers you stopped speaking aloud.
But the God of Exodus is not indifferent to the suffering of His people.
He sees.
He hears.
He knows.
And in His appointed time, He acts.
Yet the next thing God said changed everything.
He was going to deliver Israel.
And He was sending Moses.
“Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.” — Exodus 3:10, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The man who fled Pharaoh was being commanded to return to Pharaoh.
The man whose attempt to intervene had ended in bloodshed was being sent to confront a kingdom.
The shepherd who had spent decades far from Egypt was being called into the very place associated with his deepest failure.
And Moses responded with the first objection.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?” — Exodus 3:11, KJV
Who am I?
It sounds humble.
And there was a legitimate reason for Moses to recognize his inadequacy.
He was not powerful enough to overthrow Egypt.
He had no army.
No throne.
No political authority.
But notice God's answer.
He did not give Moses a motivational speech about his hidden greatness.
He did not say, “Moses, believe in yourself.”
He said:
“Certainly I will be with thee.” — Exodus 3:12, KJV
In Hebrew:
כִּי־אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ — kî-ʾehyeh ʿimmākh
“For I will be with you.”
God answered Moses' question about personal inadequacy with a promise of divine presence.
Moses asked, “Who am I?”
God's answer redirected his attention toward the One who was sending him.
And that distinction matters.
Biblical courage is not pretending you are strong.
It is trusting the Lord when your own strength is insufficient.
But Moses was not finished.
He wanted to know what to say when the Israelites asked for the name of the God who had sent him.
God answered with one of the most profound revelations in Scripture.
“I AM THAT I AM.” — Exodus 3:14, KJV
The Hebrew is:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — ʾehyeh ʾasher ʾehyeh
Traditionally translated “I AM THAT I AM,” the expression can also be rendered “I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
The Hebrew verb ʾehyeh is related to the verb “to be.” The wording conveys God's self-identification in a way that resists reducing Him to a creature dependent on something outside Himself.
The surrounding context matters.
God had already told Moses, “I will be with you,” using that same verbal form.
And in Exodus 3:15, God identifies Himself by His covenant name, represented in Hebrew by the four letters יהוה — YHWH, often rendered “LORD” in English Bibles.
This is not a magical phrase Moses could use to control God.
It is God's revelation of Himself as the covenant-keeping Lord who would be faithful to His promises.
Egypt had its rulers.
Egypt had its gods.
Egypt had its armies.
But Moses was being sent by the Lord of heaven and earth.
And still, Moses objected.
In Exodus 4:1, he said:
“But, behold, they will not believe me, nor hearken unto my voice.”
This was not an imaginary concern.
Moses had already experienced rejection from his own people.
The memory of that earlier question—“Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?”—may have remained painfully relevant.
God did not dismiss the concern.
He gave Moses signs.
His shepherd's staff became a serpent.
When Moses took it by the tail at God's command, it became a staff again.
His hand became leprous in appearance and was then restored.
God also told him of a sign involving water from the Nile becoming blood.
These signs were not party tricks.
They were divine attestations that Moses was being sent by the Lord.
The God who commanded him was demonstrating His authority over creation, disease, and the river associated with Egypt's life and power.
Yet Moses had another objection.
“O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” — Exodus 4:10, KJV
The Hebrew describes him as:
כְבַד־פֶּה וּכְבַד לָשׁוֹן — khevad-peh u-khevad lashon
Literally, “heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue.”
We should be careful here.
Scripture does not establish a specific medical diagnosis or prove that Moses had a particular speech disorder.
His words communicate a perceived difficulty with speaking, whether involving fluency, ability, confidence, or some combination of these.
And God responded with a question.
“Who hath made man's mouth?” — Exodus 4:11, KJV
Then came another promise.
“Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.” — Exodus 4:12, KJV
There it was again.
God's presence.
Not merely with Moses on the journey.
With his mouth.
With the very weakness he had placed before God.
How often do we ask God to remove every limitation before we obey Him?
We want confidence before speaking.
Certainty before moving.
Healing before serving.
A perfect past before offering testimony.
We want the entire road illuminated before taking the first step.
But God had not promised Moses an easy assignment.
He had promised to accompany him.
And there is a world of difference.
Then came the sentence that changed the atmosphere.
After every answer, every reassurance, every sign, and every promise, Moses said:
“O my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send.” — Exodus 4:13, KJV
That wording in the King James Version can sound confusing to modern readers.
The Hebrew is:
שְׁלַח־נָא בְּיַד־תִּשְׁלָח — shelach-na beyad-tishlach
Its sense is commonly understood as a plea for God to send someone else.
Moses was no longer simply asking who God was.
He was no longer asking how the Israelites would recognize his authority.
He was no longer asking what to do about his speaking limitations.
He was asking to be excused from the assignment.
And then:
“And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses.” — Exodus 4:14, KJV
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּחַר־אַף יְהוָה בְּמֹשֶׁה — vayyichar-ʾaf YHWH be-Mosheh
The expression vayyichar-ʾaf is a Hebrew idiom for anger being kindled or becoming hot.
The Bible is not describing God as losing control like an impatient human being.
It is revealing His real displeasure at Moses' continued resistance.
And that should sober us.
Because the passage does not teach that God becomes angry whenever someone is afraid, confused, or honestly struggling.
He had just spent the conversation answering Moses' concerns.
The decisive issue was his resistance to God's command after repeated assurances.
There is a difference between bringing your fear to God and using your fear to justify refusing Him.
There is a difference between asking for wisdom and endlessly postponing obedience.
There is a difference between admitting weakness and treating weakness as greater than God's faithfulness.
And sometimes, if we are willing to be painfully honest, we know which one we are doing.
You know that person you need to forgive.
You know that sin you keep defending.
You know that apology you keep delaying.
You know that truth you refuse to face because facing it would require change.
Perhaps the Holy Spirit has been convicting you through Scripture, through wise counsel, and through the quiet discomfort of a conscience that will not let you rest.
And every time, you find another reason to wait.
Not today.
Not yet.
When I am stronger.
When I am less afraid.
When I have more money.
When people stop judging me.
When my circumstances improve.
But what if the question is no longer whether you have enough information?
What if the question is whether you are willing to obey the truth you already understand?
Do not misunderstand this.
Not every difficult feeling is a divine command.
Not every opportunity is God's calling.
Not every delay is disobedience.
Scripture calls us to test what we hear, seek wisdom, and distinguish God's revealed will from our own assumptions.

But where God has clearly spoken, particularly concerning repentance, truthfulness, forgiveness, holiness, love, and faith in Christ, we must not turn uncertainty into an endless refuge from obedience.
And here is something extraordinary about what happened next.
God became angry.
But He did not abandon Moses.
He spoke about Aaron, Moses' brother.
Aaron could speak well.
He was already coming to meet Moses.
God would instruct Moses, Moses would communicate to Aaron, and Aaron would serve as his spokesman.
Moses would still carry the staff.
Moses would still confront Pharaoh.
Moses would still participate in the deliverance God had appointed.
God's anger was real.
His command remained.
And His provision continued.
Do not turn that into the false promise that disobedience never has consequences.
It does.
But neither should you miss the mercy in this scene.
The Lord did not choose Moses because Moses was fearless.
He did not choose him because his past was spotless.
He did not choose him because his speech was impressive.
And when Moses resisted, the Lord did not surrender His purpose to Moses' objections.
The deliverance of Israel would ultimately display God's glory, not Moses' natural brilliance.
This is where the story becomes more than a lesson about leadership.
Because Moses' greatest problem was never simply his mouth.
And ours is not always the weakness we keep mentioning.
Sometimes we are terrified that obedience will expose us.
That God will send us back to the very place where we failed.
That the people who knew us before repentance will refuse to believe we have changed.
That we will try again and discover we are still inadequate.
And so we hide in familiar places.
We call isolation peace.
We call compromise survival.
We call spiritual passivity waiting on God's timing.
We call our fear discernment, even when we have not seriously sought His wisdom.
And all the while, the Lord's Word continues to confront us.
Not because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
But because He calls people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
There is another part of Exodus 4 that cannot be ignored.
After Moses finally departed toward Egypt, Scripture records a startling encounter on the journey.
In Exodus 4:24–26, the Lord confronted Moses in an episode involving circumcision and Zipporah.
The passage is difficult, and interpreters differ over certain details, including precisely whom the Lord threatened to kill.
But the episode clearly warns us against treating covenant obligations lightly.
The man sent to confront Pharaoh was not free to disregard obedience in his own household.
Public ministry does not excuse private disobedience.
A calling does not make someone immune to correction.
And being used by God is never permission to live carelessly before Him.
That is a warning for every preacher, teacher, ministry leader, parent, and believer who has learned how to speak about holiness without allowing God's Word to examine the hidden places of the heart.
We can build a religious appearance while avoiding repentance.
We can speak about surrender while keeping certain rooms of our lives locked.
We can become skilled at describing grace while refusing the transformation grace teaches us to pursue.
But God's mercy is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Grace does not merely comfort us in sin.
Grace teaches us to turn from it.
And now we must look beyond Moses.
Because if this story ends with “Stop making excuses and be more courageous,” we have not yet reached its deepest Christian significance.
Moses was a servant whom God used to lead Israel out of bondage.
But Moses was not the ultimate Redeemer.
The Exodus itself points us toward a greater deliverance.
A greater Mediator.
A greater Savior.
Jesus Christ.
Moses feared going back to Egypt.
Jesus willingly entered a world of suffering and rejection.
Moses repeatedly objected to his commission.
Jesus, in the agony of Gethsemane, prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
We must not flatten the difference between these two scenes.
Moses' resistance was met with divine anger.
Jesus' anguish was the sinless suffering of the obedient Son.
Christ was not rebelling against the Father.
He was expressing the real horror of the cup before Him while perfectly submitting to the Father's will.
That distinction makes His obedience even more precious.
He knew what awaited Him.
Betrayal.
Abandonment.
False accusations.
Mockery.
Scourging.
Crucifixion.
And He went forward.
Not because suffering was easy.
Not because the cross was painless.
But because He came to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.
Philippians 2:8 declares that He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
Moses was sent to confront the earthly oppressor of God's people.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins.
Moses led Israel through the sea.
Jesus brings His people from death to life.
Moses was a faithful servant in God's house.
Jesus is the Son over God's house.
Hebrews 3:1–6 makes that distinction clear.
And John 1:17 declares:
“For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.”
This does not mean God lacked grace in the Old Testament.
The Lord who rescued Israel was already gracious, merciful, and faithful to His covenant.
It means the fullness of God's saving revelation has come in Jesus Christ.
The One to whom Moses' ministry ultimately points has arrived.
And He does more than command sinners to improve.
He saves sinners who cannot save themselves.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you can finally become brave enough to deserve God's love.
Not that your obedience can erase the guilt of your past.
Not that your ministry, generosity, or religious activity can purchase forgiveness.
But that Jesus Christ lived in perfect righteousness, died for sinners, and rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and new life by God's grace.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Then the next verse tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
We do not obey to purchase redemption.
We obey because the Redeemer has claimed us.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this has been desperately trying to understand.
You have spent years believing your past disqualifies you from being loved by God.
You remember what you did.
The relationship you destroyed.
The person you betrayed.
The addiction you concealed.
The season when you deliberately turned your back on everything you knew was right.
You remember the words you cannot take back.
The opportunities you wasted.
The prayers you stopped praying because shame convinced you heaven was tired of hearing your voice.
And when you read about Moses, you recognize the wilderness.
Not because your story is identical to his.
But because you know what it means to feel like the person you once were has ruined the person you might have become.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
Your choices matter.
Repentance is necessary.
Some consequences may remain even after forgiveness.
But Jesus Christ is able to save sinners.
His cross is not too weak for your guilt.
His resurrection is not too small for your hopelessness.
His mercy is not exhausted by the length of your wilderness.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have the authority to overrule the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
The Apostle Paul once persecuted the church.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
The thief on the cross had no lifetime of religious accomplishments to present.
Their stories are different, and Scripture does not promise every believer the same earthly calling or outcome.
But each reminds us that salvation rests on God's mercy, not human worthiness.
And if you belong to Christ, your identity is no longer defined by the final verdict of your worst moment.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It means something more fundamental has happened.
You have been reconciled to God through Christ.
And now your life belongs to Him.
Perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending.
Not to perform repentance for an audience.
But to become honest before the Lord who already knows.
You do not have to disclose private sins, painful details, or anything that would put you at risk. God hears the confession you make to Him even when nobody else sees it.
Someone reading may need to know that repentance is possible.
That restoration is real.
That grace is not a religious slogan.
That Jesus still saves.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting alone with the same question Moses asked.
Who am I?
Who am I to begin again?
Who am I to serve God after what I have done?
Who am I to believe He could still use my life?
And the Gospel directs us away from confidence in ourselves and toward confidence in Christ.
He is the Savior.
He is the Mediator.
He is the One who deserves the glory.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality cult.
Not to make human approval the measure of spiritual fruit.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep placing biblical truth before people who desperately need the Word of God in a world overflowing with noise.
Some people will never enter a church building because they are afraid of being judged.
Some are struggling believers who have stopped opening their Bibles.
Some are parents praying for wandering children.
Some are young adults quietly losing their faith.
Some are unbelievers who have never seriously understood what Jesus accomplished on the cross.
And sometimes an article shared on Facebook becomes the unexpected doorway to a conversation about Christ.
Not because a social media post has the power to save anyone.
Only God saves.
But He can use the faithful proclamation of His Word to bring people face-to-face with the Gospel.
That is why sharing matters.
Not merely as an endorsement of a page.
But because someone in your circle may be quietly wrestling with the very excuses Moses made.
Someone who feels disqualified.
Someone who believes their past is the end of their story.
Someone who needs to hear that Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers genuine forgiveness.
And if one particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness, or sending the article privately if that would be more thoughtful.
Let the message become a bridge, not a weapon.
Return to Exodus 3–4 when fear starts speaking louder than God's promises.
Read the chapters for yourself.
Examine the context.
Pray over what the Lord has actually said.
Do not settle for an emotional moment when Scripture is inviting you into a life of faithfulness.
The goal is not simply another follower count.
It is to keep opening the Scriptures together, pointing to Jesus Christ, encouraging repentance, strengthening faith, and reminding weary souls that God's truth deserves more than a passing glance.
There is also a deeper opportunity for those who want to help sustain this work.
And for those who understand giving as an act of worship, there is a biblical way to approach this invitation.
Scripture teaches generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply.
You are free to give.
You are also free not to.
And salvation is never for sale.
These are practical ways to support and enjoy the ministry's resources, but the greatest value we hope to offer will always be the biblical truth that points people toward Jesus.
Those resources are there to help believers study Scripture, grow in discernment, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, and mature in their walk with Jesus Christ.
If you are serious about spiritual growth, explore them.
If you know a believer who cannot afford books, tell them about the free library.
But do not allow even good religious activity to distract you from the personal question at the heart of this passage.
What is God calling you to obey according to His Word?
Not what impressive thing can you do to make people admire your faith.
Not what dramatic testimony can you manufacture.
Not how can you appear more spiritual than everyone around you.
What truth has Scripture already placed before you?
Perhaps it is time to confess a sin instead of concealing it.
Perhaps it is time to seek reconciliation where doing so is safe and appropriate.
Perhaps it is time to stop excusing bitterness.
Perhaps it is time to return to prayer.
Perhaps it is time to seek the help of mature believers because you cannot overcome a destructive pattern by pretending it does not exist.
Perhaps it is time to open your Bible again after months of avoiding it.
Or perhaps you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ at all.
You know Christian language.
You know religious traditions.
You know how to appear respectful toward God.
But deep inside, you have never surrendered your hope of saving yourself.
Hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Turn from sin.
Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Trust His finished work, not your own righteousness.
Receive the forgiveness and new life that God gives through His Son.
And then follow Him.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggles.
Not without needing daily grace.
But sincerely.
Because the Christian life is not a performance of self-sufficiency.
It is a life of dependence upon the Savior who loved us and gave Himself for us.
When Moses finally went back toward Egypt, he did not carry an army.
He carried a staff.
He carried God's command.
And he went under the promise of God's presence.
The road ahead was not easy.
Pharaoh resisted.
The suffering of the Israelites initially intensified.
Moses himself would cry out to God in distress.
The Exodus would require the mighty intervention of the Lord.
But the story would not end with Moses' excuses.
It would move forward through God's faithfulness.
And that is the final contrast worth remembering.
Moses was not the hero because he never hesitated.
He hesitated repeatedly.
He was not the deliverer because he possessed extraordinary power.
The power belonged to God.
He was not the answer to Israel's deepest spiritual need.
That answer would ultimately be revealed in Jesus Christ.
The Lord who met Moses in the wilderness was faithful to His covenant.
And the same God has made known His saving grace in His Son.
So when you think about the burning bush, do not merely picture a man standing before a fire that refused to die.
Picture a frightened servant hearing the voice of the holy God.
Picture the excuses falling one by one.
Picture the terrible seriousness of resisting the Lord.
Picture the mercy that provided help even after divine anger was kindled.
And then lift your eyes to the cross.
Because there you see something Moses' story could only anticipate.
The perfectly obedient Son giving Himself for sinners.
The innocent Christ bearing the judgment our sins deserve.
The crucified Savior rising victorious from the grave.
The Redeemer who does not simply offer another chance to try harder, but gives new life to those who trust Him.
This is why the story matters.
It is not ultimately about convincing yourself that you can become another Moses.
It is about recognizing your need for the God who called Moses and the Savior to whom the Scriptures bear witness.
And perhaps, after reading all of this, your most important response will not be a public declaration.
Perhaps it will be a quiet prayer.

“Lord, I have been afraid. I have made excuses. I have hidden behind my weaknesses. I have treated my comfort as more important than obedience. Forgive me for my sins. Teach me to trust Your Word. Help me follow Jesus Christ faithfully. Give me courage where You have commanded me to act, humility where I need correction, and wisdom where I need guidance. Let my life bring glory to You. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if you have a testimony of how Christ met you in a season of failure, fear, or repentance, share what you can. Your story may encourage another person to seek the Lord.
But above all, do not leave with admiration for Moses while overlooking Jesus.
Moses stood before a burning bush and discovered that God's calling was greater than his excuses.
At Calvary, we discover something infinitely greater.
The grace of Jesus Christ is sufficient to save those who could never rescue themselves.
And if you remember only one thing from this story, remember this:
The most tragic thing would not be that you once ran from God, but that you heard His call to repentance, saw the mercy offered in Jesus Christ, and still chose to keep running.
